title: Leg 45 — Columbia River to Mount St. Helens
subtitle: Portland and Vancouver, Kalama, Mount St. Helens, Spirit Lake, Cowlitz Valley and Chehalis

blocks.title: North from Aurora toward the Columbia
blocks.text: We are leaving Aurora and continuing north through the Willamette lowlands toward the Columbia River. For a while the route is almost due north, with the Portland metropolitan area gradually building off the right side. The broad agricultural ground below will give way to denser suburbs, highways and river crossings before we reach Washington. If Mount Hood is visible in the distance, it will be well beyond Portland to the right and makes a useful reference for the east side of the valley.

blocks.title: Portland helped name Springfield
blocks.text: The largest urban area off our right is Portland, about five miles from the route. If you are trying to pick it out, look for the dense city around the Willamette River as it runs north toward the Columbia. Here is the pop-culture connection: Simpsons creator Matt Groening grew up in Portland, and local names followed him into the show. Flanders, Lovejoy, Quimby and Terwilliger all echo Portland streets or landmarks, and Groening grew up on a street called Evergreen Terrace.

blocks.title: A surprise landing from Moscow
blocks.text: As the Columbia River comes into view, Vancouver, Washington is about six miles off the right. A useful visual anchor is the big Interstate 5 crossing of the Columbia; just east of that bridge on the north bank is the short runway of Pearson Field beside Fort Vancouver. In 1937, three Soviet aviators unexpectedly landed there after flying nonstop from Moscow over the North Pole. Their ANT-25 had been aiming much farther south, but an oil-pressure problem forced the historic first transpolar flight to end at Vancouver instead.

blocks.title: Ridgefield's floodplain refuge
blocks.text: The patchwork of wetlands and open ground to the right, between the Columbia and the developed corridor near Ridgefield, includes Ridgefield National Wildlife Refuge. It was established in 1965 especially for wintering dusky Canada geese and now protects marshes, meadows, floodplain forest and oak habitat. From the air, the refuge is easier to recognize as a broad wetland landscape than as a single landmark, so use the Columbia River itself as the main pointer.

blocks.title: Woodland, the Lewis River and a volcano ahead
blocks.text: Woodland is several miles off the right near the Lewis River, and this is where the character of the trip starts changing. The long north-south Interstate 5 corridor remains an easy visual guide, while the Columbia stays farther left. Ahead, Mount St. Helens should begin to stand apart from the surrounding ridges. Unlike the more symmetrical Cascade cones, its missing north side gives it a distinctive truncated profile once the angle is right.

blocks.title: Kalama on the Columbia
blocks.text: Kalama is coming up directly on the Columbia River at our first waypoint. The waterfront is the easiest way to find it: look for the port, docks and industrial buildings gathered along the east bank of the broad river. Kalama has long been tied to river and rail transportation, but it also has a surprisingly good celebrity story. In September 1962, Elvis Presley stopped here while traveling to Seattle to film It Happened at the World's Fair, and word spread quickly enough to bring a crowd to his hotel.

blocks.title: Kalama's 140-foot piece of public art
blocks.text: Before Kalama drops behind us, one more local oddity is worth mentioning. For decades the waterfront was marked by a 140-foot cedar totem pole carved by Chief Don Lelooska. The Port of Kalama is careful to describe it as a commissioned art piece rather than a traditional Cowlitz cultural pole. Weather eventually forced it down, and after restoration it was preserved indoors as the centerpiece of the waterfront's Mountain Timber Market.

blocks.title: The mountain that no longer has a north face
blocks.text: Mount St. Helens is now the obvious target ahead. Use the mountain itself rather than any town as your visual anchor: the route is aimed almost directly toward the crater. Before 1980, St. Helens had a much more graceful, snow-covered cone and stood about thirteen hundred feet higher. The modern horseshoe-shaped crater opens to the north, which is the side we will cross immediately afterward on the short hop to Spirit Lake.

blocks.title: Two months of warning — but not the kind anyone expected
blocks.text: The 1980 crisis began with earthquakes and small explosions in March. By mid-May, more than ten thousand earthquakes had shaken the volcano and its north flank had bulged outward by more than four hundred fifty feet as magma pushed inside. Scientists knew a major eruption was possible, but the decisive event came sideways rather than simply upward. A magnitude 5.1 earthquake on May eighteenth triggered the collapse of the unstable north flank and uncorked the volcano.

blocks.title: The volcano that became a television event
blocks.spokenLabel: Waypoint Two at Mount St. Helens
blocks.text: Mount St. Helens unfolded in the age of television, and the weeks of earthquakes, steam blasts and evacuation arguments turned the mountain into a national story before the main eruption even happened. When the north side collapsed, the lateral blast raced outward at more than three hundred miles per hour and devastated roughly two hundred thirty square miles. Fifty-seven people died. The summit ahead is not merely a crater rim; it is the edge of the enormous landslide scar left by that morning.

blocks.title: Crossing the Mount St. Helens crater
blocks.text: We are closing on the crater now. The missing north flank should make the mountain look almost open toward us, with the crater floor and younger lava domes inside if the simulator's terrain detail and lighting cooperate. The May 1980 landslide was the largest debris avalanche in recorded history, and much of that material swept west into the North Fork Toutle River valley. After this waypoint, Spirit Lake is only a few miles beyond the north rim.

blocks.title: Johnston, Truman and Spirit Lake
blocks.text: This is a very short leg, so look just beyond the open north side of the crater for Spirit Lake. USGS volcanologist David Johnston was monitoring the volcano from a ridge north of here when the collapse began; his last radio call was, 'Vancouver, Vancouver, this is it.' At Spirit Lake, lodge owner Harry Truman had become a national media personality for refusing to evacuate. Both men were among the fifty-seven people killed. The eruption drove a massive wave across Spirit Lake and radically reshaped the basin we are approaching.

blocks.title: Spirit Lake's floating forest
blocks.text: Spirit Lake still carries one of the most visible signatures of the eruption: an immense mat of floating logs, trees stripped from the surrounding slopes and swept into the water in 1980. If the simulator renders them at all, they would be concentrated along parts of the lake rather than looking like an ordinary shoreline feature. The eruption also blocked the lake's natural outlet, so engineers later bored an eighty-five-hundred-foot tunnel through bedrock to keep the water at a safer level.

blocks.title: The blast zone became a giant natural laboratory
blocks.text: As we leave Spirit Lake, look across the broad gray-green landscape north and west of the volcano rather than for a single landmark. Scientists initially saw what appeared to be nearly complete destruction, but recovery began from surprising survivors: seeds under snow, roots below the surface, insects, fungi and even pocket gophers protected underground. Mount St. Helens became a remarkable natural laboratory for watching ecosystems rebuild themselves without simply smoothing or replanting the entire blast zone.

blocks.title: Follow the pale scar of the Toutle
blocks.text: The broad, sediment-filled valley trending west-northwest is the North Fork Toutle River system, and it is one of the best visual guides on this part of the route. The 1980 debris avalanche buried miles of this valley, and erosion has kept feeding extraordinary amounts of sediment downstream ever since. A large sediment-retention structure was built across the river to trap part of that load before it reaches the lower Toutle, the Cowlitz and eventually the Columbia.

blocks.title: From volcanic debris into the Cowlitz Valley
blocks.spokenLabel: Waypoint Four in the Cowlitz River Valley
blocks.text: The Cowlitz River valley is coming up at our fourth waypoint. Try to identify the winding river first; farther west, the straighter Interstate 5 corridor and the small town of Toledo provide a second reference. Mount St. Helens sediment is not just an old story here. The Toutle still carries far more sediment than it did before 1980, and managing that material remains part of flood protection for downstream communities along the Cowlitz.

blocks.title: Toledo and the river corridor
blocks.text: Leaving the Cowlitz waypoint, Toledo is several miles off the left as the river bends through the lowlands. For visual orientation, the Cowlitz is the irregular natural line; Interstate 5 is the much straighter north-south corridor farther west. We are now leaving the immediate Mount St. Helens landscape and entering the chain of small communities that links the Cowlitz country with Chehalis and Centralia.

blocks.title: Winlock and the world's largest egg
blocks.text: Winlock is about five miles off the left near the Interstate 5 corridor. You will not pick out its landmark from six thousand feet, but it is too good a local oddity to skip: the town is home to what it calls the World's Largest Egg, a twelve-foot-long, twelve-hundred-pound roadside monument to the area's poultry history. This is exactly the sort of landmark that makes much more sense from the ground than from the cockpit.

blocks.title: Centralia was founded by George Washington — really
blocks.text: Centralia will be the larger town cluster just beyond our destination airport. Its founder really was named George Washington. He was the son of an enslaved father, traveled west after facing discriminatory laws in the Midwest, and with his wife platted the town in 1875. Centralia grew into a rail and highway junction and later promoted itself as the Hub City, a name that makes sense when you look at the transportation corridors converging below.

blocks.title: A modern-dance pioneer from Centralia
blocks.text: Centralia also produced a major figure from a completely different world. Merce Cunningham was born here in 1919 and became one of the most influential American choreographers of the twentieth century, known for experimenting with chance, technology and unconventional relationships between music and dance. For the arrival, look for the airport in the low ground between Chehalis to the south and Centralia to the north, close to the Interstate 5 corridor.
